The post Review: Titan by Arctic Zone 30 Can Collapsible Backpack Cooler With Ice Walls appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Portable coolers are not new, but the collapsible backpack variety is starting to make a more noticeable dent into this category. That’s where the Titan line of soft-sided coolers by Arctic Zone comes in. Arctic Zone was founded in 1986 and have been “driven by one mission: build insulated gear that outperforms expectations.” We road tested their 30 Can Collapsible Backpack Cooler With Ice Walls, the latest in their robust line of insulated gear made for being on the move. 

There needs a framing of the use case of the Titan around this particular small-framed 5’3″ Drinkhacker writer, which puts a higher bar on weight and shape for “portability.” I will lead my review with the double spoiler alert that the 5-pound weight at empty is a bit of a drag (literally) and is the only relevant ding to expect in my once-over. 

A cooler has literally one job — which is to keep things cold for as long as possible. That was my primary angle for my review which led me to conclude that tossing in 3 lbs of frozen ground beef that I needed defrosted eventually would be a very instructive approach (and self-serving). In went the bricks of vacuum sealed meat into the cavernous pouch, zipped up and perched on a window where it was guaranteed to be beaten down by direct sunlight for a few hours. 

The findings: After 6 hours, the ground beef was still solidly frozen to its very edges. (That pasta bolognese will need to be saved for another night). And this was without the ice packs inserted into the ice walls. After 24 hours, some of the edges softened. After 30 hours, it was pliable enough, and there was proof enough of the Titan’s chilling performance, and half-frozen was defrosted enough, to cease the experiment and start on that bolognese. 

Now that I’d had my makeshift way with putting the Titan to the test, it was time to turn to the bold claims outlined on the company’s their website: 

  • 30 Can Capacity: Large main compartment holds drinks, food, and ice for group outings or long days.
  • Deep Freeze Performance Insulation with Therma-Flect radiant barrier interior keeps ice for up to 2 days.
  • Leak proof, easy clean lining with Microban protection. Spills stay inside the cooler.
  • Smart Storage & Extras. Insulated front pocket for snacks, 2 mesh accessory pockets, plus a removable bottle opener.
  • Comfortable & Durable Design. Adjustable padded backpack straps and a water and stain repellent exterior built for everyday adventures.

The compartment is indeed large and with the material’s flexibility, it can accommodate all kinds of shapes and sizes of items, packed inside like misshapen Jenga bricks. Two full days of keeping ice might be a slight stretch but the 3 lbs of beef in my experiment took up only 20% of the available space — and cooled itself without additional frozen items. Add in the ice packs, and it’s credible to me that if the compartment was even at 80%, that contents would stay at near original temperature for 2 days. 

The backpack itself is very smartly designed and very cool in all the ways. It fits comfortably on the back and has a clasp on the straps that help steady the pack against your body. However, reverting to this particular reviewer’s idiosyncrasies, I would have preferred a strap at the base of the bag so that it secured at the hip and not across the chest. As mentioned, the bag already comes in at 5 lbs empty which means if I were to go on at least a two-day excursion where cold beverages would be the chef’s kiss at a summit, I’d make sure there was a sturdier companion to volunteer to be my sherpa. Because that sunset view over the canyon with an icy cold one with chilled charcuterie would actually be nice. 

A / $90 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

The post Review: Patron 100 Silver Tequila appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Unlike a lot of recently released tequilas, this new expression from Patron doesn’t exactly reinvent the wheel. It’s a 100 proof version of its classic blanco, made using the same 100% agave, 100% tahona production techniques, and bottled in a traditional Patron decanter. No additives, just a higher abv — and, intriguingly, it is distilled to proof, with no dilution after the fact.

Patron 100 Silver Tequila Review

If you like Patron at 80 proof I expect you’ll like it just as much at 100 proof, though as with the original Patron, this remains a simple, straightforward expression. Lime leads the way on the nose, and, enhanced by the added alcohol, it’s even more prominent than in standard Patron. Peppery and quite yeasty, time in glass helps the tequila to build out a bready character, though always quite racy with a big citrus edge.

The palate fires up with some heat, with lime leaf again very prominent. This serves to temper some of the more agave-forward elements of traditional Patron, but only just so. The experience turns green and a bit vegetal after the citrus notes die down. From there, a tenacious white pepper character builds, adding spice to a thick layer of roasted agave notes, quite woody and increasingly earthy as the finish approaches.

The extra alcohol gives this blanco a dimension that 80-proof Patron seems to lack, if only slightly; the heavy lime character makes it perfect for more aggressive margaritas and Mexican martinis.

100 proof.

B+ / $50 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: 3 South American Bordeaux-Style Red Blends, 2026 Releases
summary:

Are we talking Left Bank or Right? Which of the traditional cast of grapes survived the audition,…

The post Review: 3 South American Bordeaux-Style Red Blends, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
To label a wine a “Bordeaux-Style Red Blend” is to make a promise in the manner of a politician: confident in tone, possibly vacant in substance, and dependent on an unwillingness by the audience to ask follow-up questions. Are we talking Left Bank or Right? Which of the traditional cast of grapes survived the audition, and which were dismissed without notice? What understudy has slipped onto the stage, hoping no one checks the program? In South America, the sleight of hand is so routine it barely qualifies as deception: wherever Bordeaux’s ghost is invoked, look for Malbec standing in Merlot’s coat, hoping to be mistaken for the original. Here are three blends willing to test how far the mimicry can be stretched.

2023 Bodegas Salentein Numina Gran Corte Valle de Uco — A blend of  60% Malbec, 20% Cabernet Sauvignon, 7.5% Cabernet Franc, 7.5% Petit Verdot and 5% Merlot, a formula that keeps the fab five on the payroll, even if most of them are working part-time and phoning it in. Raspberry and red currant open the proceedings, giving way to a full-bodied run of blackberry, cedar plank, and tobacco leaf. This is the sort of wine that doesn’t need the borrowed prestige of a French appellation to make its case, though it will happily take the free advertising. A- / $50

2022 VINUV Memoir Grand Reserve — 60% Merlot, 20% Cabernet Franc, 10% Malbec, 5% Cabernet Sauvignon, 5% Syrah, aged two years in French oak and another two in the bottle. Merlot offers vanilla and plum up front, supported by a full-bodied stretch of dark fruit and cherry behind it in good balance. An aged Gouda or Manchego would not go amiss as a candidate for pairing. B+ / $64

2023 Alta Vista Atemporal Valle de Uco — 60% Malbec, 30% Cabernet Sauvignon, 10% Petit Verdot, aged twelve months in French oak. The nose offers violet, pepper, cinnamon, and licorice as it settles, determined to provide some dimension. On the palate, Malbec supplies the silk, Cabernet Sauvignon the spine, Petit Verdot the volume, and remarkably no one grape tries to filibuster the others. B / $25

title: Review: Spirits of Charbay, 2026 Releases
summary:
While distiller Marko Karakasevic has been often occupied with his side hustle at Wolves Whiskey, his original baby, Charbay, continues to roll along as the OG producer of whiskeys made from beer alongside dropping some impressive vodkas and liqueurs. It’s been seven years since our last review of a Charbay product, so recently, the brand…

The post Review: Spirits of Charbay, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
While distiller Marko Karakasevic has been often occupied with his side hustle at Wolves Whiskey, his original baby, Charbay, continues to roll along as the OG producer of whiskeys made from beer alongside dropping some impressive vodkas and liqueurs. It’s been seven years since our last review of a Charbay product, so recently, the brand got in touch and suggested we revisit some old friends and become acquainted with some new ones, sending us a collection of products that span a good amount of its production.

We’ll break down the details in each writeup of the six products tasted below. Let’s dig in.

Charbay R5 Final Lot (2026) Review

We’ve reviewed R5 four previous times (including its inaugural launch in unaged form); this is the first we’ve seen under the revamped label, which officially drops “Hop Flavored Whiskey” from the name. It also adds a more ominous note — “Final Lot” — to the label, an unsubtle message that this is the last production run for the expression. 10 barrels were produced for this batch, which was distilled from Racer 5 beer in 2017 and aged in oak for 6 1/2 years before bottling.

The song really remains the same this time around, nosing both with ample fruit and a ton of eucalyptus and pine notes, exuding aromas of the fresh hops that are so iconic in Racer 5. There’s even more fruit on the palate, which quickly tempers the bitterness of the hops and runs to apple and lighter orange notes, followed by a more ephemeral floral influence and touches of anise. There’s quite a bit of mint in the mix, giving the whiskey more of a wintry vibe, although it’s so light on the palate that it works well in the dead of summer too, particularly with water or a fizzy mixer. Sad to see it go! 99 proof. A- / $55 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Charbay S Hop Flavored Whiskey Lot 2 (2026) Review

Charbay S is distilled from the (now discontinued) hop-infused Bear Republic Big Bear Black Stout, and we last saw it billed as Lot 211A. This version, Lot 2, is aged for nearly twice as long as the previous version of this whiskey — 50 months in French oak barrels instead of 29. As expected, this is a more soothing, luscious expression than R5, with biting notes of pine and citrus peel on the nose, chased by rich florals and undulating aromas of coconut nectar, brown sugar, and gravelly barrel char.

The palate takes all of the above and pushes it through a significant note of chocolate and coffee, with earthy hops ringing the edges of the experience — never overwhelming, never even dominant. The finish maintains the chocolate-caramel focus, with elements of Turkish rug shop and macerated cherries weaving in and out of view. It’s the same whiskey as the old Charbay S, but better integrated and more cohesive. I went back to the well on this far more than I expected to. 99 proof. A- / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Charbay Doubled & Twisted Lot 3 (2026) Review

Doubled & Twisted was once a light whiskey that was, in fact, Charbay’s first ever release back in 2011. It has evolved since then into a complex blend of Charbay’s other whiskeys, now comprised of 20% 2013 Charbay R5, 20% 2017 Charbay R5, 40% 2015 Czech Pilsner whiskey, 10% 2011 Charbay S, and 10% 2012 California Single Malt whiskey (considerably different than our last encounter). So, is this just a blend of leftovers? I don’t think that’s a bad way to look at it, but then again I absolutely love leftovers for lunch.

The nose is inviting in a way that D&T hasn’t really been before, offering layered butterscotch and shortbread biscuit notes, touched with brighter punches of baking spice, orange peel, citrusy hops, and chai. The palate follows in lockstep but feels more ephemeral, with layers of vanilla settling over the experience as that creamy chai note comes further into prominence. While it’s a tiny portion of the blend, the Charbay S feels like it dominates the experience here, with touches of chocolate and caramel that I just couldn’t shake lingering forever on the finish.

I’ve dismissed Doubled & Twisted in the past, but this latest rendition is more than worthwhile. (And available for a song.) 90 proof. A- / $40 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Charbay Blood Orange Vodka (2026) Review

A vodka we’ve seen twice; while originally macerated for 6 months, it’s now got a 90 day extraction of blood orange mandarins. A delightful shade of orange, the fresh citrus notes explode forth from the glass upon pouring, offering a big punch of bittersweet fruit that effectively mixes juice and peel. A not insignificant note of vanilla sugar brightens the vodka up as the finish approaches, though as I have noted previously, it takes a sharp U-turn at the end of the experience, dropping some bitter, mouth-puckering astringency. You won’t find many 80 proof orange-flavored vodkas on the market, however. 80 proof. B+ / $30 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Charbay Espresso Martini Review

The first canned cocktail we’ve seen from Charbay, this is a ready-to-drink espresso martini made with cane neutral spirits, real espresso, real vanilla, and simple syrup. Immediately upon cracking open a can, the cocktail comes across as aggressive. The nose feels rather burnt, like slightly scorched coffee, leading to aromas of very dark chocolate and a little wood smoke. The palate, fortunately, is cleaner and more engaging thanks to a palpable sweetness paired with an aggressive coffee character. Caramel notes promise to soothe the finish, though these too come across as a bit burnt, with overtoasted coconut clinging to the gritty, slightly acrid back end. 30 proof. 2 servings per can. B / $12 per four-pack of 200ml cans

Charbay Nostalgie Black Walnut Liqueur Review

From a family recipe, this is an extraction of black and English walnuts that spends about a year steeping in alcohol before spices and sugar are added to finish the experience. The liqueur has the bold nuttiness you would expect and hope for, lightly winey with overtones of cherry. The walnut meanders toward pistachio with lacings of chocolate and, in the end, a significant baking spice character that melds with a slightly earthy molasses sweetness. Delightfully well-balanced and expressive without being over the top. I also love that it comes in half bottles. 60 proof. A / $60 (375ml)

title: Review: 2025 Quinta da Fonte Souto Florao White
summary:

Not much has changed across the Portuguese landscape (save perhaps a new label that buries “Branco” description in favor of the more internationally friendly “White.” There’s still the balance…

The post Review: 2025 Quinta da Fonte Souto Florao White appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Depending on the time of publication, we will have passed the one-year mark since trying the 2024 vintage of Portugal/Symington’s Quinta da Fonte Souto Florao White. Not much has changed across the Portuguese landscape (save perhaps a new label that buries “Branco” description in favor of the more internationally friendly “White.” There’s still the balance of old world and new, still the same opportunity to dine at amazing spots and enjoy stunning art from some of the world’s most original voices. Ronaldo and Bruno have yet to win a World Cup.

So, too, goes the wine world of Portugal, which hasn’t experienced any seismic shifts. There are still enjoyable options in plentiful abundance. Today, we’re checking to see if Quinta still retains a spot on the roster of quality options at a sensible price point, or if this white blend from Alto Alentejo has been downgraded, needing to find a seat on the bench.

This 75%/25% blend of Arinto and Verdelho offers aromas of white flowers and grated lemon zest with a touch of nut brittle as it evolves. On the palate, grapefruit and lemon zest seize nearly all control, filibustering from first sip to last with minimal interest in yielding to anything else in the blend. It’s medium-bodied but “soft” isn’t in its vocabulary: it has edge and the acidic equivalent of good posture, but never crosses into something aggressive. Orange blossom shows up on the finish, but a mild touch of salinity cuts towards the conclusion, keeping the whole wine approachable. This year’s vintage has fully retained its charm and quality, and remains one of the better affordable Portuguese white wines available.

B+ / $21

title: Review: Deanston Orange Wine Cask Finish 17 Years Old
summary:
Whoever bet on sleepy Deanston to have one of the most ambitious experimental whisky collections, step right up and claim your prize. After Virgin Oak, Tequila Cask, and Organic Oak releases, the Highland distillery has dropped its latest Experimental Whisky, this one finished in Vino de Naranja casks (which Deanston confusingly refers to as Orange…

The post Review: Deanston Orange Wine Cask Finish 17 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Whoever bet on sleepy Deanston to have one of the most ambitious experimental whisky collections, step right up and claim your prize. After Virgin Oak, Tequila Cask, and Organic Oak releases, the Highland distillery has dropped its latest Experimental Whisky, this one finished in Vino de Naranja casks (which Deanston confusingly refers to as Orange Wine).

The whisky spends 15 years in ex-bourbon barrels before its two years of finishing in Vino de Naranja barrels. For those unfamiliar, unlike modern orange wine (essentially a type of rose table wine), Vino de Naranja is a Spanish fortified wine made with the infusion of bitter orange peels. Technically it can also be described as an “orange wine,” and I’m sure that term looks more enticing (and understandable) on the label than “Vino de Naranja” does. So, Deanston is forgiven.

7000 bottles were produced for this release, and we got a small taste. Let’s dig in.

Deanston Orange Wine Cask Finish 17 Years Old Review

The intense citrus on the nose here immediately recalls a sherried Speyside single malt, with its prominent, almost biting orange influence. Cinnamon and cardamom add a distinctly spicy element, with some peppermint aromas building with time in glass.

Rich and a little funky on the palate, loads of fresh orange marmalade await the drinker, amplified by those same spice notes backing it all up. It’s perhaps a bit one-note — Vino de Naranja will do that to a delicate whisky — but it’s a note that works well, slowly emerging as a rather beautiful whisky despite some initial brutishness. The reasonably high abv gives the finish some kick, menthol and a pinch of pepper offering a bracing, almost cleansing conclusion.

107.2 proof.

A- / $132

title: Tasting Report: The Energy Drinks of Alani Nu
summary:
Alani Nu, arriving as it does in cans the colors and designs of Lisa Frank Trapper Keepers, is merely the latest entrant in a tradition stretching back through the patent-medicine wagons of the nineteenth century to the “vitamin tonics” hawked on AM radio in the 1950s. However, what distinguishes Alani Nu isn’t the formula of…

The post Tasting Report: The Energy Drinks of Alani Nu appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Alani Nu, arriving as it does in cans the colors and designs of Lisa Frank Trapper Keepers, is merely the latest entrant in a tradition stretching back through the patent-medicine wagons of the nineteenth century to the “vitamin tonics” hawked on AM radio in the 1950s. However, what distinguishes Alani Nu isn’t the formula of caffeine and the usual alchemical promises of “focus” and “energy”, but its audience. The genius of its marketing lies in its familiarity with the youth demographic, resplendent in all of its Gen Z technicolor vigor, and its ability to hit some flavors right on the mark with uncanny accuracy. We tried nearly every available flavor on the market, including two new seasonal releases, for this report.

Alani Nu Cherry Slush – A bit of a one-note deal, but what a note it is. Of all the Alanii (Alanis?) sampled for this review, this comes the closest to an actual slush straight from a summer childhood. Put it over ice or serve cold, and it’s wholly reminiscent of the melted syrup and ice combo at the bottom of a large cherry Slurpee, absent the brain freeze. One of the best of the cohort currently on offer. A-

Alani Nu Sherbet Swirl – A blend of orange, raspberry and lime, which also happens to be the order in which each arrives and departs. The balance is correct between sweet and savory, forgoing the threat of becoming excessively cloying, while also invoking a slightly creamy finish. This was another dangerously drinkable one, and if the caffeine content wouldn’t send me shooting through the roof like a cartoon Coyote on a rocket, an additional can wouldn’t be out of the question and awfully tempting. A-

Alani Nu Voodoo Vanilla – One of three seasonal items for Autumn 2026 and the first for Alani’s Elixir series, this is an 8-ounce sipper with lower caffeine levels meant to be mixed with another drink of your choice as part of the dirty soda trend. I can attest that this works well with some (Witch’s Brew, Cherry Slush) more than others. However, the vanilla and marshmallow running throughout make it drinkable as a standalone. B+

Alani Nu Witch’s Brew – Double, double toil and trouble, fire burn and caldron bubble: the second of the three (we did not receive the third, Ruby Apple) makes its return to the stage for 2026, and it is definitely green caramel apple. It is very heavy on the caramel part of the program but mercifully recedes during the final act, as the green apple takes over with a surprising touch of lemon zest making a cameo. Which is certainly an improvement over wool of bat, tongue of dog, eye of newt or toe of frog. B+

Alani Nu Orange Kiss – Most Alanii sprint straight to dessert-tier sweetness and never look back. This one laces up its sour shoes and jogs in the other direction, landing on a citrus flavor resembling citrus instead of a chemistry lab’s idea of it. The result tastes uncannily like orange soda. Or “pop,” for anyone raised correctly, in the parts of the country where language still makes sense and nobody’s out here calling it “soda” like a degenerate. B+

Alani Nu Blue Slush – Classic gas station Blue Icee and shockingly accurate despite the fact there is an absence of sugar. Somehow Alani gets the formula spot on for almost all of their Slush variations (more on that below). So if that excessive blue raspberry onslaught isn’t your thing, it may be better to sit this one out. However, this satisfies that childhood cravings effectively. B+

Alani Nu Cosmic Stardust – This one is a bit of a mystery. One minute it’s grape soda bordering on Dimetapp, the next sip it’s a mouthful of Skittles. I can’t fully confirm either, but what I can confirm is that there may be a segment of the population that would find this flavor appealing, and I get that. But I am not one of them. Not the worst of the batch but needs a bit of retooling to be a top-tier choice. Adding some mixer elixir helps. B

Alani Nu Juicy Peach – Quite syrupy and unctuous up front. However, as it simmers down toward the end, the lingering peach mellows and resembles peach nectar. Good in small doses, but after a while the whole affair just coats the mouth excessively. B

Alani Nu Watermelon Wave – After drinking several different offerings that verge on cloying, this presents as surprisingly light. It doesn’t evoke watermelon Jolly Rancher as anticipated, but presents more like a watermelon spritz mocktail. In fact, this
would function well as a mixer, with or without the alcohol, if drinks by the pool are the order of the day. B

Alani Nu Cherry Twist – The twist here is that it is a cherry-lime hybrid. But the real twist is how much it resembles cough medicine. The cherry dominates throughout, leaving no room for the lime to even really cut through. It’s not wholly unpleasant, as it does eventually settle down on the finish, but it’s quite a big challenge to overcome. Unless using this as a mixer, skip and proceed to Cherry Slush instead. C

Alani Nu Pink Slush – A merciless onslaught of strawberry bubble gum and cotton candy at first, with a cream soda finish preventing it from being fully undrinkable. Unlike others, this leans in too hard on the candy store heaviness. Some retooling to stand with its Blue and Cherry Siblings is not out of the question. C-

$23 per 12-pack of 12 oz cans [BUY THEM NOW FROM AMAZON]

title: Review: E. Leon Jimenes 1903 Ron Dominicano
summary:
E. Leon Jimenes has been known as a cigar producer in the Dominican Republic since 1903, and over 100 years later (in 2013), the brand branched out into a natural complement: rum. E. Leon Jimenes makes its two rum expressions from pure cane juice instead of molasses and distills on a column still on the…

The post Review: E. Leon Jimenes 1903 Ron Dominicano appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
E. Leon Jimenes has been known as a cigar producer in the Dominican Republic since 1903, and over 100 years later (in 2013), the brand branched out into a natural complement: rum.

E. Leon Jimenes makes its two rum expressions from pure cane juice instead of molasses and distills on a column still on the island. It does not add sugar to its products and it ages them linearly, not in a solera style. During an online tasting (and cigar and cocktail pairing), we tasted Jimenes’s latest release, 1903, an 8 year old offering that spends 6 1/2 years in ex-bourbon barrels and 1 1/2 years in sherry barrels before bottling.

E. Leon Jimenes 1903 Ron Dominicano Review

The rum noses with a slightly industrial character, owing likely to the heavy sherry influence on the spirit. Time in glass helps this to evaporate a bit, ultimately revealing a sharper fruit aroma — orange peels in syrup and cherry, though all of it comes across as a little leathery, with overtones of oxidized wine.

The palate is fairly light in body, the pungency of the sherry influence waning a bit, though the experience becomes quite nutty at the jump. A bold milk chocolate character is unmistakable, followed by a dance of spices — anise, nutmeg, lumbering notes of coconut and toasted sesame. Again the sherry messes with expectations, the finish taking you on an increasingly winey trip, culminating in a creamy layer of orange flower water. Normally I prefer rums with a lot more body than this — which can feel a little watery at times — but the unique flavor profile drew me in over and over again.

80 proof.

B+ / $45

I didn’t smoke the cigars from La Aurora, the Dominican Republic’s oldest cigar producer, but will report back with an update to this post when I do.

As for the cocktail, it’s a spin on a dark and stormy, made with Mabi Seibano, which is the Dominican Republic’s answer to root beer — a bit sweeter and more floral. (You can find it on Amazon.) Fun little cocktail — and very spicy, so be prepared for some merengue to break out.

Tormenta Quisqueyana

2 oz. E. Leon Jimenes 1903 Rum
3 oz. Mabi Seibano
1 oz. ginger beer
1/2 oz. fresh lime juice
1/4 oz. demerara syrup

Build over fresh ice in a chilled highball glass. Stir gently. Garnish with a dash of cinnamon or a cinnamon stick.

title: Review: Sauvy B by Joel Gott Wine Spritzers
summary:
We are pleased to report another winery has entered the fray to rescue wine from the ready-to-drink wilderness: a lawless, inflamed expanse where vodka mascots, venture capitalists, and seltzer bros have been quietly eating wine’s lunch for years while wine sat there, uncanned, slowly withering an analog death. Enter Joel and Sarah Gott, who surveyed…

The post Review: Sauvy B by Joel Gott Wine Spritzers appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We are pleased to report another winery has entered the fray to rescue wine from the ready-to-drink wilderness: a lawless, inflamed expanse where vodka mascots, venture capitalists, and seltzer bros have been quietly eating wine’s lunch for years while wine sat there, uncanned, slowly withering an analog death. Enter Joel and Sarah Gott, who surveyed the entire farm-to-canned-cocktail-industrial complex and thought: what if instead of vodka, jalapeños and shame, we canned Sauvignon Blanc and gave it a personality upgrade? The result is Sauvy B, a spritzer which takes their actual wine (two guesses which varietal), dilutes it with natural citrus flavor, hits it with sparkling water, and seasons the whole situation with electrolytes via Himalayan pink salt, presumably mined by yaks under a full moon and blessed by a wellness influencer before it touches the can.

It’s not so much a beverage as a mood board: aspirational and engineered for people who own a cooler bag than yours, presumably with someone’s monogram on it. I could be wrong, but I’m not sure if anyone asked for electrolytes or Himalayan pink salt in their spritzer. But the blessed free market provides, whether or not you were thirsty for pink Himalayan salted anything, and here we all are, cracking a few open anyway.

Sauvy B by Joel Gott Lime – The intended flavor here is on point, without the chemical or excessive artificial sweetener notes usually lurking about with drinks of this sort. It does exactly as advertised with a burst of lime that is relentless throughout. The actual Sauvy doesn’t really appear until the finish, but none of this matters much, because the thing is dangerously easy to drink, the kind of easy that can empty a four-pack in a day if you’re not careful. Serve it up with graham crackers or butter cookies for a proper dessert session, helping to take the sweet edge off ever so slightly. I was prepared to be a hater, but this turned out to be a pleasant surprise. A-

Sauvy B by Joel Gott Grapefruit – Much like the lime, this is full grapefruit for the entire runtime, and the Sauvy makes a brief cameo. Unlike the lime, the Himalayan pink salt overstays its welcome in the best way, lingering on the back end after everyone else has gone home. If you’re drinking from the can, a few swirls around helps things a bit, and if you’re drinking from a glass, an ice cube or two isn’t out of the question. Either way, it’s still very drinkable and makes one respect the Gott’s instinct to season a spritzer with rock salt from a mountain range and somehow get it right. B+

each $14 per four-pack of 12 oz cans

The post Review: AJ Bond Tennessee Whiskey appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
David already got the full backstory on AJ Bond when he talked last month with whisky-maker Allisa Henley. We discovered in that interview that she was the ‘A’ in AJ Bond, with the ‘J’ being the late John Lunn, a veteran of George Dickel, like Allisa, who joined Sazerac in 2016 when the company purchased their then employer Avery Trail Distillery and set in motion grand plans to give Jack and George a run for their money.

In 2017, I had the chance to taste some of Allisa’s and John’s earliest experiments at WhiskyFest in Washington, DC. The brand didn’t even exist yet, but I remember being impressed with where things were heading. It was entirely unlike the banana- and peanut-filled white dog of those other big Tennessee whiskey producers. Distilling operations reportedly moved to La Vergne in 2019, but then Lunn passed suddenly in 2023, casting doubt on whether we’d ever taste a final product. It was a welcome surprise to hear the news earlier this year that, after nearly a decade in the works, AJ Bond had finally arrived.

As with their many other whiskeys, Sazerac doesn’t give us any details about the mashbill, but we know a little something about the process. Most unique, AJ Bond is a blend of pot and column-distilled whiskeys. Initial distillations were on Avery Trail’s pot stills which were modified to support the pre-barreling charcoal filtration required to certify as a Tennessee whiskey. In 2021, a column still came online. There’s no age statement, but we’re told this first release is a blend of those younger column-distilled whiskeys with pot-distilled stock that is pushing a healthy 8-9 years old. And to pack as much Tennessee into the bottle as possible, corn is sourced locally from Murfreesboro while maturation occurs in Tennessee-grown white oak. We’ve been waiting a long time for this one. Let’s check it out.

AJ Bond Straight Tennessee Whiskey Review

The aroma showcases some classic Tennessee whiskey elements, but it does so with a unique depth and richness that speaks to the maturity of the whiskey but also the pot distillation. Notes of caramel corn, vanilla, cocoa powder, and maple fudge offer up a gentle sweetness restrained by undertones of barrel char, subtle woodsmoke, and damp earth. As it opens, that darker vanilla bean note becomes a little higher toned, blooming into cream soda and cake frosting.

When David interviewed Allisa, she made it clear that the goal for AJ Bond was to be a more approachable, sipping Tennessee whiskey. On the palate, they’ve certainly achieved that – perhaps to a fault. Initial notes of brown sugar and maple candies are light and a touch thin at the outset, building with some intensity across the sip and delivering almost too much easy sweetness. Maple syrup and vanilla extract on the midpalate continue the saccharine trend before some slightly savory contrast arrives in the form of creamed corn and honey roasted peanuts. A flourish of cracked pepper, barrel char, and dark chocolate further tame things on the finish, but the fadeout is still generously sweet with notes of buttercream icing, cinnamon syrup, and graham cracker. It’s an impressive foray into Tennessee whiskey for Sazerac; a Tennessee whiskey that does indeed stand apart from Jack and George. AJ Bond should find plenty of admirers, especially at this price point.

95 proof.

B+ / $35
